utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So good morning. Mr. Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-03-68-T, the Prosecutor versus Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Oric, I would like to know if you can receive interpretation in your own language?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. Yes, yes, I can receive -- I do receive interpretation in my own language, and I can follow the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. If there are any problems at any time, let me know. You may sit down. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I'm Patricia Sellers of the Prosecution, with co-counsel Mr. Gramsci Di Fazio, and Ms. Donnica Henry-Frijlink is our case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I thank you, and good morning to you and your team. Appearances for Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. My name is Vasvija Vidovic, and together with Mr. John Jones, I appear for Mr. Naser Oric. With us are our legal assistant, Ms. Jasmina Cosic, and our CaseMap manager, Mr. Geoff Roberts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, madam, and good morning to you and your team. Any preliminaries, or any follow-up to the matters that I raised yesterday with regard to witnesses? MR. DI FAZIO: Yes, if Your Honours please. I've prepared a little working document which I see over there on the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We don't have it. MR. DI FAZIO: Can you just distribute it? Thank you. It's not actually quite what it says because it doesn't go into early January. I'll deal with that last entry later. Essentially, it's what I think is going to happen between now and the end of the year, the Christmas break. And it's a little less ambitious than the other schedules that we had, but I think this is slightly more realistic. The times that we have here are -- I've included both examination-in-chief and cross-examination times. So when I -- when you see the evidence of a particular witness, that's all of their evidence, both examination-in-chief and cross-examination. So if we start today, it's self-evident what we have today. If we finish at some point about three-quarters of the way down today's track, then we can start with the next witness, as you can see. And then tomorrow is self-evident; we're not sitting. I'm told that that particular witness who may start today and finish on Thursday is a reasonably substantial witness, not just a very minor crime-base witness, if I can say that, and that's why I've --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You have allocated to him the entire day of Tuesday -- Thursday. MR. DI FAZIO: Thursday, essentially, yes. Then Friday, I'm confident that we should complete that witness safely, and then we enter the last week of Christmas -- before our Christmas break. Monday, the 13th, we have the witness who's to be recalled. I would suggest that we, no matter what the state of play is, that he be interposed, if necessary. I would hope that it would not be necessary, and I would have thought that we would have finished the previous witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Two hours? MR. DI FAZIO: Do Your Honours think that's an overestimate?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think so. MR. DI FAZIO: Well, if it is, it won't significantly affect this schedule in any event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: And then we could start with the -- that other witness and finish him on the Tuesday. That would leave one last witness. I've structured it that way to make sure that we don't have any witnesses from the former Yugoslavia here on the Friday giving their evidence with the risk that we may run into running into the break and then having to call them back, which would be a real inconvenience for everyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: And then finally, finish the evidence on the Friday, the last day of court, with Racine Manas, who is working here. So even if we don't finish her evidence, and I would think we would, but even if something untoward were to happen and we don't finish her, it's no problem to call her back to complete her after the Christmas break. So that's -- I don't know what Your Honours think of that, but I think that's realistic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It seems okay to me. I want feedback, if there is, on the part of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I think that's all right, Your Honour, because in the case of Witness Eric, we need to show some documents to him which we need him to comment on, and these have to do with what we saw on the video. This will take about an hour and a quarter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Judge Brydensholt, do you ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Judge Eser? Yes. Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: There's only one matter now and that remains the opening, re-opening of the case, as I understand the the court sittings recommence on Monday the 10th. Friday the 7th, the preceding Friday, is the Orthodox Christmas, and of course that will affect all of our --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But not all the witnesses are Orthodox, no? MR. DI FAZIO: No. No, that is so. No, they're not, Your Honour is correct. Most of them are, though. Most of the crime-base witnesses are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Most of them are, but there are witnesses that aren't. MR. DI FAZIO: No, no -- they're mainly experts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are there any witnesses left that are based here in The Hague; for example, the photographer? I don't know. MR. DI FAZIO: Just let me consult with my colleagues, if Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, let's do it this way, because I've been here long enough to know what we expect. If all the other Chambers or Trial Chambers are not sitting on the 10th because of the problems that the Orthodox Christmas poses to the transfer of witnesses, then of course we will not try to be the only ones to sit. I mean, it doesn't make sense. However, if there is a number of Trial Chambers sitting on the 10th of January, which I would expect there would be, then perhaps -- then perhaps you could, between now and when we go into recess on the -- after the sitting of the 17th, find out if you could bring someone else who is not Orthodox, who hasn't got to come from ex-Yugoslavia and -- MR. DI FAZIO: Well, I'll make inquiries, as you suggest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of course, if you have problems, no one is going to try and be difficult. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes, Your Honour. Well, what I suggest is that we make our inquiries -- what I suggest is that we make our inquiries, and perhaps we can revisit this issue before we break up. Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm told that there are two cases that day, on the 10th. We could also sit in the afternoon, if necessary, which would also give you more time to -- but anyway, see what -- because I also take it that you also need your staff to have your holidays as well, like we need. So I'm not trying to be difficult. Don't -- MR. DI FAZIO: It's not actually that problem, if Your Honours please. Members of the team will be back before this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Even we are going to be back. MR. DI FAZIO: It's a question of actually getting people here to proof and continue. But I'll look into it, and if we revisit the issue again before we break, that should fix it, I hope.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. Just so that we can also make best use of the break, we would be grateful to receive a list, obviously, of the witnesses who will be coming in January as soon as possible so we can prepare for them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I was coming precisely to that, and also to -- so that, I suppose, I don't need to repeat. You will look into that and furnish the Defence and ourselves as well with the list of witnesses you intend to bring over in January. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes, I'll do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: As things are, and considering the momentum that we have been keeping, which is exceptionally good, I must say, when do you reckon you would finish your case? MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, I haven't given that any -- I haven't prepared to address you on that. I can certainly do so. If you want me to work out a time again, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you, say, on the last day before we go into recess, you give us a rough indication, I think that would be very useful for everyone. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. We will prepare something for the Trial Chamber. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because there are some days in the end of January and mid-March, when we will need to have a very short break, so more or less we will need an indication from you, all right? And thank you for all the good work you have been doing, Mr. Di Fazio. Any other preliminary matters? None? Usher, please, the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Mr. Nikolic, and welcome back. I hope you have had time to rest. This morning we are going to proceed with your testimony and hopefully finish within the next two, three hours. So relax, sit down. And may I just remind you that you are testifying, you are giving evidence on the basis of the solemn declaration that you entered yesterday, which is still valid today, in other words.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, if at any time there are problems with interpretation, if you're not receiving interpretation in your language at any time, please draw my attention immediately.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So you had another 15 minutes, starting with the video, if I remember well, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. I'll only propose to show the first portion of the video, because other witnesses will be able to comment on the remainder. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, it will be shown without sound, there is no need for the sound, and I'll just ask this witness to comment on various scenes that are depicted in the video. Examined by Mr. Di Fazio: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, I'm going to show you this video, and from time to time I'll stop it, and I'll ask you to tell the Trial Chamber what the video shows. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let's just play it now.

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the post office in Srebrenica. The police station. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that the entrance that you were taken through into your custody when you were first taken to Srebrenica, or were you taken in through another entrance?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Continue.

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recognise that place?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police station. That's the entrance to the upper floor.

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about that room? Do you know what that room is?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The duty room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's on the right-hand side of the entrance to the police station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Continue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know where those stairs lead to?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These stairs lead upstairs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think that's -- thank you for that. Okay. Now, do you know where that corridor is?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's in the police station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, just look carefully there, is the cell in which you were incarcerated with Kostadin, or Kojo, and the other man called Mica, is the door to that cell visible there? Is it one of those four doors that you can see, or is it elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's on the left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So one of those two doors that you can see on the left --

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- is that the door to the cell that you were kept in when you were first captured and taken to Srebrenica? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Continue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What's that place?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is our cell where we were incarcerated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You testified yesterday that people were able to stick -- push sticks in other instruments through the -- through the bars and hit you. Are they the bars you were talking about?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Continue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There's that room with the blue walls. Do you know where that room was, now that you're looking at it through the video?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember. I think this is in the old police station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. It appears to be part of a lavatory there. Does that jog your memory at all or not? If you're not sure, that's fine. Don't --

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. We'll continue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, is this building abandoned now or what? MR. DI FAZIO: I don't know what the current status is now, but it looks pretty abandoned --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It looks pretty abandoned there. But what's the state of it now? MR. DI FAZIO: I simply don't know, if Your Honours please. I can find out and let Your Honours know. Just pause there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What does that show?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the window, and there are doors to the left and to the right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. If you kept walking down that corridor, would you come down the front of the building or the back; do you know?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You'd have to go to the back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Keep going.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know which door that is?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The door to the old police station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is that the door that you said that you were led through after you had been captured?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the door on the ground floor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Continue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recognise that building?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the old police station, the SUP, the stairs leading to the upper floor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber how you were led, how you were taken from one building to the other when you were transferred? Were you escorted by policemen? How far away was the old police station to the municipal building?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When they transferred us from the police station to the prison between the court and the municipality, they escorted us from behind. The distance is about 300 metres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just remind the Trial Chamber, when did that transfer take place in relation to the arrival of prisoners from Skelani? Can you hear me? Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Di Fazio, there must be some problem, because I looked into his eyes and I don't think he was following. Could you repeat your question, please. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When were you transferred from the MUP -- sorry, the SUP building to the municipality -- to the prison located behind the municipality building? When was that in relation to the arrival of the prisoners from Skelani?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was right away then, because on the 16th and the 17th, when they arrived within a day or two, they transferred us to the prison, because it was very cramped there, it was two by two. And then they transferred us to the prison.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the cell that we saw a few minutes ago with the bars in front of it, for a period of time, a short period of time, there was you; Kojo, or Kostadin; Mica; and the prisoners from Skelani all placed in that cell; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then you were all transferred.

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's carry on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What entrance can we see there on the left?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the old police station, on the left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, just on that particular shot that you can see there, on the right-hand side, the extreme right-hand side, there's a building you can just see with a red roof. What building is that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the municipal assembly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where was your second prison in relation to that building?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Between the court and the municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Just continue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, that laneway, where did that lead to?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this is the municipality, and this is the prison where I was incarcerated, I think.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mean at the end of that laneway, the little road that we can see that's blocked by the two cars?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The lane, yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recognise that little yard and the building with the bars on the window?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that the second prison that you were kept at?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is the window to your cell or prison area depicted in that particular shot?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No? Where was it? Where was the window to your cell?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was at the top of the building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you mean on the ground floor or on another floor altogether, on the second floor?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was on the ground floor, because there was no upper floor here, there was only one floor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you're saying that the window to your cell is not seen there.

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Continue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, does this show the interior of the building of the second prison?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us if you can see the room where the women were kept and where the men were kept. If you see it, don't omit to mention it. Remember that you're looking for the cell where the women were kept and where the men were kept. Just let the Trial Chamber know if you can see it. If you can't, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were straight ahead through the corridor, and the women were to our left. That's the entrance. And the women were on the left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, this particular shot that we can see shows a corridor with a door at the very end. Just go slowly and tell the Trial Chamber where your cell was, if you -- where the door to your cell was, if you can see it in that shot.

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Straight ahead. Our door was straight ahead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So the one that you can see open and with the light coming through it, if you walked into that room, you would walk into the very room in which you were kept; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And what about the women? Where were they kept?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the left, the door on the left-hand side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. There are two doors on the left-hand side. Is it the door on the left-hand side closest to your room, your cell, or is it the one Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond furthest away, the one closest to us as we look?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were the second door from our cell. I know because I carried firewood there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Yes. Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recognise that room?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, that's as far as I need to go with that particular video. We have other witnesses who may comment on it. Thank you. If Your Honours please, I seek to tender into evidence the entire video. It has ERN number V000-5026. Copies are here, and I ask that it be tendered into evidence and given an exhibit number. And if Your Honours please, that completes my examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, just one matter for this exhibit. Obviously, it would be helpful to know when it was filmed, and by whom. We assume that this will be given in evidence at some point. MR. DI FAZIO: I can inform you that it was taken by an investigator of our team. If we can -- just apparently last summer. So if we can give the particulars to the Defence, perhaps we can just simply agree that as a fact, if that's convenient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay with you, Mr. Jones?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We concede that with the Prosecution. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So, Mr. Nikolic, the Prosecution has finished with its -- with their questions, and you are now going to be cross-examined by Mr. Jones for the Defence. Mr. Jones. We haven't given a number to the exhibit, to the video. I think it already has -- it's premarked 446, I think. Yes, this video that was made use of in the course of the last part of the examination-in-chief has been premarked as P446, and is being admitted with that reference number. So it becomes Prosecution Exhibit P446. Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Cross-examined by Mr. Jones:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, good morning.

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to start by asking you some questions about the area where you were living in 1992/1993. Now, you told us yesterday that Siljkovici is 300 to 400 metres from Zonjici your village, your hamlet.

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, that's not right, is it? Even as the crow flies, it's more like two or three kilometres from Siljkovici to Zonjici?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Siljkovici and Zonjici, it's like this, if you draw a vertical line and look straight down that vertical line -- and then as the crow flies, I never really measured this. It was a rough estimate. I may go wrong by a couple of yards, but not much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I wouldn't pursue it much further, Mr. Jones. What I think is happening is if this is Siljkovici, and this is Zonjici, what he's referring is the distance from the tip and the other tip, so basically --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's also what I'm referring to, Your Honour, and we say that's at least three kilometres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will try and go on site and see it with our own eyes. I wouldn't worry too much about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Of course I mean to continue. It was simply to get an answer from the witness. It's something which maps will verify the distance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But I think you're not on the same wavelength. I think he's understanding one thing and you're understanding another, so the way he's measuring it. So don't worry about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Nikolic, you're not going to suggest, are you, that you can see what people are wearing in Siljkovici from Zonjici, are you?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes what? Yes what? Because I don't know how your question was translated --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I can rephrase it. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, are you saying that you can -- when you're in Zonjici, you can see what people are wearing in Siljkovici?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, how long would it take you to walk from Zonjici to Kravica, roughly?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if my health was okay, not more than 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then how long to walk from Zonjici to Siljkovici?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would take longer to go to Kravica. Siljkovici is up the hill, and it's three times the distance because it's up the hill, so you can't fast.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So to walk from Zonjici to Siljkovici could be, what, an hour's work or something like that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would not be necessary. A healthy man can walk the distance in half an hour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you were asked some questions yesterday about the village guard, so I'm going to pursue that with you briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And with the usher's assistance, I'm going to pass out a new document, and also, if possible, I'd like this map to be on the ELMO at the same time. This document, for the record, it's from the Bratunac collection. The document -- this is an extract from a document which is 105 pages document, and the ERN of the whole document is 0065-6757 up until 0065-6861. And the whole document, from which these are extracts, consists of lists, receipts and salaries from August 1992. And that's why we have the first page 0065-6765, because that shows August 1992. And then we pass to the extracts which I'm going to be using with this witness. And I've asked for the map to be on the ELMO just so we can see some of the places as we go along.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Nikolic, if you could look at the document that's been put in front of you, flip through it, you'll see references to Donji Bacici, Gornji Bacici, Marici, Brezanci, Siljkovici. These are all places in the Kravica commune, aren't they, or community, your neighbourhood; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you were asked yesterday about the village guard, "seoska straza," and I'm going to come to that in a minute. But firstly, I want to draw your attention to page 0065-6774, and then we see "interventni vod." Do you know what that is, the "interventni vod"?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. This village guard that you referred to. I have no idea what else it could be.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But have you heard as the "interventni vod" as a unit which specialised in ambushing and killing Muslims as they tried to move about the area?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you heard of the commander Drago Cupo Djuric? Do you know him?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd ask you to look through this document, and you'll see that, taking the first page, you have Donji Bacici, and then you have "seoska straza," village guard, beneath, and again with Gornji Bacici on the first page, a list of names, and then "seoska straza." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's right, isn't it, that the village guard is a separate entity Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond from these other units.

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, it's probably a separate entity. They guarded the village. The army should be something different, but I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I'll come back to that. Can you turn now to page 0065-6777, and it's the page with Kravica, and I'll ask you to see there the 49 names listed, and then beneath we have "strazu krugu komande," guards at the command centre. Now, are you aware of the command centre in Kravica, and where that was based?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know the army from Bratunac was there. I didn't have anything to do with them. I didn't have anything to do with the army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you see the name there under Kravica, number 39, Pajkan Gavric? Do you know him? Number 39, Pajkan Gavric.

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know him, or did you know him?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew him when we were children, but I wouldn't recognise him now. He had been away for a long time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know that he was killed on the 7th of January, 1993, at an artillery post?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you've told us that you spent the whole war in Opravdici, or near Opravdici, I believe. If you could turn to the next page, Opravdici, I want to ask you a couple of questions about that. Firstly, at number 9, "Nikolic Zoran, R.," that's your son, isn't it, number 9?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It reads Zoran Nikolic, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The "R" would be Ratko, indicating that that's his father.

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, he wasn't in the village guard, was he, because we see "seoska straza" written below. Is it right that he would have been in the VRS or in some military unit?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time he was in Loznica, in the hospital, as far as I remember, in 1992. I'm not sure what the records say about his sick leave. I don't quite remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Looking at -- looking at these other names, do you know these other people, Mile Djukanovic, and the other Djukanovics, the Gajics?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It's a rather young man. I didn't stay there for the whole time in 1992. I worked in Zvornik, and I would go to Opravdici every once in a while. But my records were kept in Mali Zvornik, in Serbia, not in the municipal assembly in Bratunac. I would go every once in a while. And then after my surgery in 1992, I went more often. I could not be in Mali Zvornik and I could not work there for I went home a lot. People almost forgot about my very existence, because I was someone who worked a lot in the field.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Looking at these names from Opravdici there, and being from that area, you know, in one form or another, all of these people, don't you? I mean, none of them are altogether unfamiliar to you. If there's anyone you don't know, perhaps you could point out their names to us.

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll tell you all the people who were over 70 -- all the people who were over 70, I know them. Zivojin, I know him. He died after the over. He was aged over 70, for example.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll move on.

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Niko Petar, I don't know him. Dukanovic, he also died. He moved to Belgrade. He was aged 93. I know that man Paja Peric --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, if I can direct your attention to the first part of the list, not the village guard, you've spoken about Mile Djukanovic and the other Djukanovics. My first question to you is: Do you know the people in the first half of the list, those first 16 names, the Djukanovics, the Gajics, Slobodan Gavric? You know those people as well, don't you?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only know Slobodan Gavric. He's an elderly person. He must be about 65 now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So he was not in the village guard, was he, if you know?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was in the village guard. I know him. But he never left the village, Slobodan Gavric. He must be aged about 60.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If he's in the village guard, why is his name not listed under the village guard? MR. DI FAZIO: Well, if Your Honours please, it's not for this man to comment on what was in the minds of the creators of this document or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I still would like to hear what the answer is going to be. I agree entirely with you, Mr. Di Fazio, but let's hear it. Do you have an explanation why his name appears here and not amongst the list of village guards?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I would ask that this document be given a Defence exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So this document is being tendered, admitted, and marked as Defence Exhibit ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, D117.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: D117, thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: Your Honours, and Mr. Jones, is this the whole document, or is this just this one page?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: The whole document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no, no. If you had followed carefully what he said in the beginning, he gave the ERN numbers, first page and last page, of the entire document. This is only a part. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm just tendering the part. MR. DI FAZIO: ... the entire bundle is the one exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What I understand is what I have in my hands is being exhibited, not the entire document.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Precisely. It's what's been handed out that's being tendered.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Nikolic, from Zonjici, you have a good view of the Kravica-Bratunac road, don't you?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You couldn't see anything between Kravica and Bratunac, between Zonjici and Bratunac. Only Kravica, that's as far as the view went. But you couldn't see any further because there's a valley there and you couldn't see a thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm speaking about the road which, in fact, goes from Konjevic Polje to Bratunac. You could see that road as it went past Kravica and on till Bratunac, couldn't you?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I could see the road from Zonjici, from my house, as far as Kravica. The distance is perhaps about 200 metres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, from the start of the war, from early 1992 onwards, you could see a lot of armoured vehicles, tanks, and that sort of thing, moving along that road, couldn't you?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Because I didn't spend all of my time there. Therefore, I was in no position to see.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were there and you looked at the road, isn't it right that you did see JNA tanks, APCs, and other military equipment moving along that road?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1992, you know what it was like. I used to work, I would come over. Whenever I was sick, I would take my livestock over to Popovica, but I didn't go over to Kravica all the time, nor did I have any reason to. I didn't have any reason to know whether APCs were driving through, tanks or lorries.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll stop you there. First of all, we don't know what it was like. That's why you're here to tell us what it was like. And secondly, the question is not whether you had reason to see anything. I'm asking you what you saw. And if your evidence is that you never saw a single tank or APC on that road, then please tell us. If you did see it, then Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond please tell us that also.

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never saw any tanks. I did see vehicles drive by, because there were lorries that were covered and they looked like some sort of a vehicle [as interpreted], but they had protection, they were covered for transport.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to move on to another document.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown D6.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, one correction for the transcript. The witness said armoured vehicles, it looked like an armoured vehicle, and what we see in the transcript is just vehicle.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because it had protection on the sides, for transport, for the protection of the passengers, protection from bullets and shooting.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the President, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, had you, in fact, used the word "armoured vehicles" or just "vehicle"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think vehicle. It's a vehicle. It's like a lorry that is covered by a tarp, a tarpaulin. I'm not sure what to call it.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, but he did use the word "armoured vehicle" and could the transcript please reflect what he is saying. I see why he's trying to explain it a different way now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Had you used the word "armoured vehicle" or not before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think what I'm telling you, how can I explain what it was like, whether it was armoured or protected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's not what I'm asking you. What I'm asking you is whether about a few minutes ago, whether you had used the word "armoured" -- the phrase "armoured vehicles."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I used the word, but I'm not sure what to call it, whether it's protected for transport. It's a lorry that is protected, it's closed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if you could look at this next document, Mr. Nikolic, and I'm going to direct your attention to the page with ERN 0665-6784, and it's got Ocenovici Banovici at the top. I think just for everyone's benefit, we can now see at the top of the map on the ELMO those places, Banovici and Ocenovici. Again, going down that list, we have a separate village guard, "seoska straza", and then Artiljerci. Now, firstly, in Artiljerci, there's a Zoran Nikolic under Artiljerci. Do you not see that? ERN 0065-6784, it's D6. Do you know Zoran Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no, but -- yes, but the father's name, because there are several people called Zoran.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Never mind there for the moment. We see artillery, and 15, maybe even 16 names there. Now, you were in the area in 1992. Did you hear artillery, heavy artillery, firing in the course of 1992 in that area?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ocenovici and Banovici is several kilometres from where I live, and I don't know anyone who lives there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That wasn't the question, Mr. Nikolic. In 1992, did you hear heavy artillery firing in your area?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your evidence is that you never in the whole time, let's take it up to the 7th of January, 1993, in that whole period, you didn't once hear a single cannon or mortar firing?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I could hear when I was back from Zvornik, in the morning. If I was at home, I would be back in the morning, and when there are sounds of shooting, there is no way for me to tell where it's coming from, Kravica, Siljkovici, Sandici, Mratinjci, I don't have any reference points. When the sound comes from somewhere deep behind, I really couldn't tell where it was coming from.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when you say "shooting," are you referring to machine-gun fire or are you referring to the fire of heavy artillery, like I say, mortars, cannons, grenades?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there are differences between infantry weapons. You can hear very strong, very loud sound. The sound is much stronger. I'm not sure what to call it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've told us you had a clear view of Siljkovici from Zonjici. Is it your evidence that you didn't see heavy artillery deployed on Siljkovici?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday, when you referred to Siljkovici, you said it was on the edge of the forrest and therefore that it probably had guards. By that, did you mean it was near the front lines?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you also said yesterday that your elder son Goran lived in Belgrade during the war, but in fact, he, too, was in the Serb military in Kravica in 1992, wasn't he? In October 1992.

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you saying no, or you don't know?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Because our people had the records like the one before, the village guard. Sometimes seven or eight people, all of them were killed. And then those that were born elsewhere, it was registered elsewhere, because those people had lists that had nothing to do with it whatsoever. Like the one before, the village guard Opravdici, I know seven or eight people, they were all killed. They were all elderly people. And they appeared to be on some records of some units or another.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when were those people killed, the seven or eight people that you've referred to?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know Zikoman Cilovic [phoen] and Rado Gajic and those other people that I've enumerated. All those people were aged over 70 years of age, they no longer exist.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When were they killed, is the question, Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they were all killed after the war, since. None of them exist any more. But I can't designate a date for you. Those were all elderly people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They were killed after the war? You mean they were murdered after the war?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, a natural death. Natural death. That's how they died. They're old people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If it was a natural death, why did you see they were killed?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, okay, that's how you say where I come from.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. If we could look at the next document, next exhibit it bears the ERN 0131-9843, again from the Bratunac collection.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry, just to clarify one point, Mr. Nikolic. The seven or eight people you referred to, they died after the war; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, turning to this next document, if you could -- if I could refer you to page, it's 0131-9862, at the top it's written "Ceta Kravica poginuli ranjeni," Kravica Company, killed and wounded." Number 2240, we see Nikolic Goran, with an R presumably for --

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I'll wait for you to put your glasses on. If you look at number 2240, it's five from the bottom, Goran R. Nikolic, and the R stands for the name of the father, doesn't it? My question for you is: That's your son, Goran, isn't it, in the Kravica Company?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. But he wasn't wounded, he was in Belgrade. I think that can be verified. He was certainly never wounded. There is a man named Goran Petrovic, Goran Djuric. I knew other kids who had the same name. But my son was never wounded, and that should be easy enough to verify.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned one of the Goran -- you say there's another Goran Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond Nikolic who you know?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know Goran Petrovic, I know Goran Djuric. Those were his schoolmates. Therefore, I really can't say. But I know that they too were fighting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The only Goran Nikolic in your area was your son; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. My son is named Goran.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So he wasn't in Belgrade but in company -- Kravica Company in October 1992.

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, yes, he was working there.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I didn't get the last part of the witness' answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In October 1992, where was your son, Goran Nikolic? Was he working in Belgrade or was he working in the Kravica unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was working in Belgrade, in Belgrade, in the company Elektro Serbija.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'd simply be asked that this document be given a number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So this document is being tendered, received, and marked as Defence Exhibit D118.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Nikolic, before your capture in January 1993, you already had a hernia problem, didn't you, and you also couldn't use your right leg.

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did use my right leg, but I had hernia. My knee wasn't painful; however, my leg became painful after I was imprisoned in Srebrenica, because my pelvic bone, something happened to my pelvic bone, and my leg is drying up now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, let's take it one step at a time. Your hernia problem was before the war and nothing to do with the war.

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1992, on the 5th of May, I was due to have surgery, but then my heart was weak --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't need to go into such detail. It's a simple question and I think you've answered it. On the day that you were arrested, you were shot in your left leg, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So at the time of your capture, you already had a hernia problem, you had been shot in your left leg, and you had some problems with your right leg, before you -- at the moment that you were captured; isn't that right? And a yes or no would suffice.

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, going to the 7th of January, 1993, I'm going to ask you about Siljkovici. You told us yesterday that the first thing you saw on the 7th of January, 1993, in the direction of Siljkovici, were flames coming from houses in the early hours, but that it wasn't light at that point. So my question is the following: You couldn't, in fact, see anything of how those houses came to be on fire, could you? You didn't see how they came to be on fire.

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only saw that the houses were burning, and I could hear shooting. They were shooting from weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you can't say for sure, can you, that people set fire to the houses rather than the houses catching fire by use of weapons during the initial assault by zoljas or grenades or mortars. That's not something you can help us with, is it?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I couldn't see that. All I could see was flames and smoke.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. And you also told us yesterday that you saw people coming down from Siljkovici but that you couldn't see what they were wearing. And my question is: Could it not be the case, therefore, that they were all in civilian clothes, all the people who came down from Siljkovici, or at least a large number of them?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw people coming down and yelling, "Charge. Catch them all alive." But it was still dark, it was only beginning to get light, so I couldn't see what clothes they had on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So those people - this is my question - could all have been civilians, as far as you know.

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say whether they were all civilians or whether they were soldiers. I couldn't see all the details because it wasn't quite light. So you couldn't actually see which of them were carrying what kind of weapon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You couldn't see if they were carrying any weapon, could you?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I couldn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you couldn't see, at that time certainly, whether they were women -- whether there were women and children among them either, could you?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the same applies, doesn't it, to Kravica. You couldn't see who, if anyone, set fire to houses in Kravica.

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you could see Kravica. It was already getting light when they started -- when the burning started.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you didn't see anyone setting fire to any house, did you?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I got back home, when my wife and son had left and I was wounded, hit in the leg, when I got back to my house, I could see two armed men and two women entering my house. So I went along the side of the house and hid in that hollow tree trunk and observed what was going on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're talking about Zonjici, though, aren't you? That's not Kravica. Your house isn't in Kravica, is it?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is your house in Kravica?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it isn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just sticking with Kravica, isn't it right that you didn't see anyone set fire to any houses in Kravica?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I couldn't see them setting fire to the houses, I only saw the houses burning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. So again, those houses could have caught fire from some non-human cause, for all you know, from grenades or mortars.

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They couldn't have, because Siljkovici had been attacked and people were running away. Nobody would set fire to their own house. Women and children were fleeing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, yesterday you referred to soldiers, but when pressed, you admitted that many of the people you saw were actually in civilian clothes. So I put it to you that actually the people you saw on the 7th of January, most of them are civilians, although some of them may have had weapons, and not soldiers at all. Is that something you'd accept?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I saw the people escorting those gathering things, looting, they were women, children, and adults, and they had to be soldiers securing them, escorting them with weapons. Who else could they have been?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They weren't wearing uniform, were they, these people.

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you on that day were in civilian clothes, I think you've told us. If you picked up a gun, would you say you were a soldier?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you told us how you hid after the attack on the 7th of January, and how during that time you saw people taking things, mostly food and livestock, so I'm going to ask you some questions about that. The people who were taking things were mostly women and children, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were elderly; they were carrying things. I didn't notice others carrying things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They had bags for putting food in, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see that. I didn't pay attention. I couldn't see every detail. I didn't have time. I didn't dare. Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you heard the expression "torbari" to describe civilians scavaging for food in this area at this time?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I never heard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see these people who you've described taking food fighting each other over the food, arguing with each other and fighting over the things they were trying to take?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had occasion to see that in the village when they were taking my things, because I was some 500 to 600 metres away. And when they were collecting my wheat from the barn, they arrived in trucks and in tractors and they were arguing. I heard them well. And in the evening when they came out, I saw that they had been drinking coffee. There was a fire burning and there was a pot used for cooking coffee still there. And they were arguing about how to share the wheat, and they were each trying to get a larger share.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. It was chaos, wasn't it, with people fighting each other over the food which was in your village.

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So I put it to you that these people were desperate, starving civilians taking what they could to survive a very bleak winter. Is that something you'd accept?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you've told us you assumed that these people were Muslims because -- well, you assumed these were Muslims, but Serbs in the area were also scavaging in the village, weren't they, because you told us you were scavaging for food yourself. So it wasn't only Muslims taking food.

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't go anywhere I had food in my own house. I didn't need to go and look for it elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you accept that Serbs from your area probably took things with them, livestock and food, from their own homes, if they had time before they left, and maybe even took things from their neighbours as well, if they had time before they left?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, maybe they did. But I can't say because I wasn't there all the time, so I couldn't see every detail. Probably they did, but I can't say whether they did or not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you even say for sure that the Muslims you've described took what belonged to the Serbs rather than -- took from the Serbs what properly can be said to have belonged to them?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think you need to rephrase the question, because --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Certainly, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- because it's quite difficult to understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't it right that Serbs in Kravica had already been stealing livestock and other goods from Muslims who were expelled from Glogova and other Muslim villages from the start of war? The transcript should read "Muslims" rather than "Serbs." Had been stealing from Serbs -- stealing from Muslims who had been expelled from Glogova and other villages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, there is an obvious mistake in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're saying that never happened, that Serbs never stole livestock or other goods from Muslims expelled from Glogova and other Muslim villages?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe they did. I'm not asserting that they didn't, but I didn't see that. I wasn't there to pay attention to everything that went on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I've got a couple more questions on this theme, and then I'll be moving on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've referred to armed people, armed men, escorting these civilians. It's right, isn't it, that your army had fled after the 7th of January, 1993, and so there were no Serbs in the area posing any danger to the Muslims there.

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they weren't there. Perhaps people were afraid and they escorted them. On Christmas, on the 7th, I was there for five days and I didn't see anyone there. If I had found someone, I would have joined them, I wouldn't have stayed there wondering about the house all on my own.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My point is this, Mr. Nikolic: That there was no need for any armed people to guard the civilians, was there, because there was no one they needed to be protected from since all the Serbs had left the area.

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But what is safe is safe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Finally, just on this subject, I put it to you that the armed people you saw weren't soldiers but simply civilians who had weapons. Would you accept that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether they were civilians or soldiers, but they were carrying weapons and they were young and able-bodied. I didn't ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I can -- we can have a break there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we'll have a 30-minute break, because we have a meeting. MR. DI FAZIO: That is exactly what I was going to ask for an extra five minutes today because I have a problem with my pass and I can't move throughout the building, I have to fix it, so that suits me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. We have a short meeting so we need 30 minutes ourselves in any case.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm much obliged, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Nikolic, you told us yesterday how on the 12th of January, 1993, you were arrested by seven armed people in civilian clothes, and that you walked to Lolici where you came upon Zulfo. Now, it's right, isn't it, that he stopped you from being molested by a large group of people who were there in Lolici.

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also told us that you boarded a minibus, a kombi, I think you referred to it as, and that the people were there in white but the rest were in civilian uniforms, or civilian clothes; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were three who were in camouflage uniforms. Only three, they were in white camouflage clothes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I want to move now to when you first entered Srebrenica, well, not first, but on the 12th of January, 1993, and I want to ask you about what you saw on the streets there when you arrived. Now, did you see very large numbers of people camping out on the streets of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw a large number of people walking about the streets. I didn't see them camping. I didn't stay there long. I just passed through. We stopped in front of the police station, and that was just a short way. It wasn't a long journey through the town so that I might see that. It was only some 50 metres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see thousands of people living on the streets of -- you've told us you didn't see them living on the streets, but in the streets, burning plastic buckets for warmth, emaciated, and that sort of thing?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't see that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you've told us that it was minus 10 degrees at some times during that winter, and I think it's right, I think you told us that there was also no electricity in the town.

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There was no electricity.

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, just to anticipate slightly, isn't it right to say that the whole time you were in prison, in both locations, that most of the time it was very dark, very hard to see anyone or anything?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you've told us how you were brought to the SUP building in Srebrenica, first of all. Is it right that the people who had arrested you handed you over to the civilian police, to the civilian authorities?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether they were civilian. They handed us over at the entrance to the building and took us to that room with the bars, where the prison was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, the people you saw at the SUP were in civilian clothes, weren't they, the people you saw there, or old police uniforms.

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. They had different kinds of clothes, as far as I could see.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As far as you could tell, these were police clothes or civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was different. All kinds. It wasn't a single colour. There were all kinds of colours. They probably changed shifts. It wasn't always the same people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you told us yesterday that you were interviewed at the SUP on the 30th of January, 1993, the next day. Now, the person who asked you questions, or the persons, was he, or they, also in civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: Just for the record, I think it's been -- I think it was a slip of the tongue. It should be the 13th of January, not 30th.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Sorry, I certainly meant to say 13th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. It's too late to correct the transcript itself, so what you have just been confirming will amount to the correction. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did you see whether the answers you were giving to this person, whether they were being noted down on a typewriter? Was someone typing the answers that you gave them, or was it being handwritten?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Handwritten, with pencil.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you were asked yesterday about certain personal details. Do you actually recall now, 11 years later, whether you were asked all of those questions, asked for all of those details, or is that something you don't remember?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, but I do have this document. Here it is, the 11th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, we can see that later. I don't want to ask you about any documents now.

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's from Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I presume the Prosecution is aware of that document, so I'm certainly not going to pursue that now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, these details which you were asked about yesterday - your wife's maiden name, where your sons were working - that's something which your friends in the Kravica area would know perfectly well, wouldn't they? These aren't secrets.

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They probably knew that, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, it's right, isn't it, that after you were released from custody, you were interviewed by Serb authorities and spoken to by the Serb authorities about your captivity in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they interview you many times?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many times did they interview you, the Serb authorities?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serb authorities didn't talk to me much. After I was exchanged, I can't really recall, I don't remember. There was that occasion when the television took pictures of me, but I can't really remember anymore.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When the authorities spoke to you, did they ask you for similar details about where you lived and where your sons lived and what your wife's maiden name was?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, on the 16th of January, 1993, the 16th or 17th of January, 1993, you told us you had transferred to another building from the SUP because too many people had arrived as a result of the fall of Skelani. So my question is: Is it right, then, that you were transferred essentially to an annex of the SUP in order to house the additional arrivals?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were -- when these people were brought from Skelani on the 16th and 17th, I don't know what sort of attack was up there. Four others were brought in as well. And a day or two later, we were transferred to between the court and the municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, when you were transferred, you shared a cell, you told us, with four people who had been kept in captivity for, I think it's right to say - and correct me if this wasn't your evidence - for seven months in a stable near Kasaba?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was Andza, Mico, Dragan, and Jakov from Kalabaci near Siljkovici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Now, they were in a very bad condition, weren't they, because of what they had suffered in those months before they arrived in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did they tell you that they had suffered a great deal before they were brought to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They told me that they hadn't had an easy time, that they were in a stable or cowshed. They spoke a little and then they kept quiet a little. They didn't speak out very much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they arrive after you or before you?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After me. In early February, that's when they arrived in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when they arrived, you could see that they were in a pretty bad condition already.

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to ask you a few questions about the beatings which you suffered, and I want to make very clear, before I ask you these questions, that we don't wish, of course, to minimise in any way what you suffered, but just to be clear about what your injuries were. So I hope that's clear.

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every day they beat us --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, I was pausing for the interpretation. So I'm about to ask you a question. If you'd wait for a question, and then if possible, just answer yes or no. Isn't it right that the injuries which you were treated for were, first of all, broken ribs, two broken ribs, I think it was, and that your ribs were broken on one specific occasion, on the 6th of February, 1993. Can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Five ribs were broken, not two. On the 6th, the evening, when they beat us three times during the night, when Kostadin Popovic and the man from Skelani died.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So that was the 6th of February. You've told us also that you suffered a cut with a knife, and you've told us about that so I won't ask you any more about that. You also mentioned that you had a loose tooth as well, that you still suffer from a loose tooth; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you all right to continue, Mr. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I can. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it's right to say, isn't it, that you weren't treated for any other injuries, apart from those injuries which you've just told us about - the ribs, and your tooth, and the cut - when you were in Zvornik Hospital.

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you do say, it's your evidence that you were beaten continuously with rifle butts, sticks, fists, feet, for 40-odd days that you were in captivity. Is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'd like to play the Prosecution's video exhibit from yesterday with a corrected transcript which we prepared. I can point out what the corrections are. They're minor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
