utterances.text: But we also need the text offered by the Prosecution so that we can --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. And you have that as a Prosecution exhibit from yesterday --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I think it's 114 and 115, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If the technical booth could prepare to play a Defence video, or a video from a Defence computer. And if you could watch and listen to the video, please, Mr. Nikolic, we'll have sound.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have it yesterday here. Have you distributed the Defence version?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. Perhaps we can play the video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If we could just pause there, because I'd like to ask Mr. Nikolic a question about that segment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it's -- in English, we have: "On 16 January, when Skelani was attacked, five more men were brought. We were there until February 6 when they beat us up. They cut me there and they cut my ear." Do you recall yourself saying that on the video which we saw just now?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I still have it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, it's right, isn't it, that you were in fact beaten for the first time on that night of the 6th of February, 1993, and that's why you say "we were there until February 6 when they beat us up," because that's the first time that that had happened.

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They had beaten us many times while we were still at the old police station. On the 6th of February, this happened in a different place of detention.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you say that in this different place of detention that you were beaten every day, as you told us yesterday, and that the people in the next cell would have heard the sounds of you being beaten every day?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The women would have heard it, would have heard the sound of you being beaten every day. Very well. We'll continue with the video.

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's the end of the video. We would be tendering the transcript into evidence and the segment of the video, if it hasn't been tendered already. I'm not quite sure what the state of play as far as that is concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Jones, before you proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: May I just have a question with regard to the difference in translation. The point which you referred to us, "we were there until February 6 when they beat us up, they cut me there, and they cut my ear." That is in your translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, the word "kada" wasn't translated in the Defence one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: And if you go back to the translation proposed by the Prosecutor, it's a different. It's: "We were there until February 6. They beat us up, they cut me here, they cut my ear." So in the Prosecutor's translation, you wouldn't have the term "when" --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Exactly. That's precisely why we thought it important to correct, because in the original, the word "kada" appears, and you'll appear in Bosnian, I won't try and repeat in Bosnian apart from this part, "kada su nas tukli" and we heard the word "kada" on the video, and Mr. Nikolic confirmed that that's what he had said on the video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: May I just ask the translator to confirm which translation is the correct one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would suggest we re-run that part of the video so that I hear it as well, and then I will ask -- I will put the question to the interpreters. I think we need to go back to the part where the witness is showing his right hand part -- side of his neck.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Our CaseMap manager is just working on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That was it, actually, that was the segment. I don't know if the interpreters can confirm they heard the word "kada."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, I have to refer to the interpreters who may have been following in the Serbian language.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The booth believes that segment is actually the next one.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: My apologies. We'll run it again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We can --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's the next bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, it's the next bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Should be play it, then?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Continue. Continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. The interpreters could --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "And we were there until the 6th of February when they beat us up."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So I put it to the witness, and perhaps I'll put it again --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think you need to put it again, because the witness gave you a clear-cut answer, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As far as who beat you, Mr. Nikolic, in the prison, isn't it right that it wasn't the guards who did it but people who broke into the prison to, as you put it, see the Chetniks. It was those people from outside who beat you.

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The instructions, the guards at the gate, they couldn't even have come in and opened the doors to our cells if they hadn't led them through. They couldn't have broken the gate down. The guards opened the gate for them, and then they would come in and beat us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't it right that the guards actually tried to stop people from breaking in and attacking you, at least on one occasion?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the guards - help us with this if you can - they were civilian policemen, weren't they? If they told you that or if you were able to see that.

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't it right that one of them had one arm and was called Zele. Perhaps not in actual prison but someone you saw subsequently.

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, we saw you yesterday with a book which I believe is "Bloody Christmas in Kravica." Now, you told us yesterday Zulfo came to the prison every day. Isn't it right that in that book, you said that Zulfo only came to the prison twice?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zulfo Tursun came almost every day, as far as I can remember, during the 46 days that I was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to ask you a few questions about Kostadin Popovic. Were you actually present when a body which was later believed to be his body was exhumed? Were you present for that exhumation?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't present. I only saw him later when Kostadin Popovic died on the 6th, and on the morning of the 7th they came. Tursun Zulfo came first at about 10.00, and he walked straight through the prison --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll stop you there, Mr. Nikolic. I'm asking about the exhumation which took place years later, I believe. The question is whether you were present, and you can answer that with a yes or no, and I think you've told us that you weren't present.

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So you don't, in fact, know, do you, whether a piece of paper with his name on it was found on the body or not. That's something other people have told you.

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's no, you don't know, and yes, other people have told you?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But when other people told me that on the photograph it said Kostadin Popovic, when they brought the stretcher in to put him onto the stretcher, the guard asked me, he brought pen and paper and he asked me about that man's name and I said, I know he is Kostadin Popovic. And then he wrapped up the paper and wrapped it in nylon; therefore, the nylon preserved this piece of paper from the water inside the earth when the man was buried.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: One moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just a minute. Before you proceed, the transcript of the relevant part from the video clip that we saw is being tendered, I suppose?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And it's being marked D119.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the reason I ask you that, Mr. Nikolic, is that we want to hear from you what you saw yourself, not what you heard from others. For that reason, I was confirming that you weren't present during the exhumation. I take it that remains your answer; you weren't there when the body was found.

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, as well as Kostadin, you said that an old man died after the 6th of February, 1993. You don't know who he was, do you? You don't know his name. And please don't refer to any documents. Mr. Nikolic, I don't wish you to refer to documents. I wish you to refer to your own recollection.

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know his name then. Later, when the documents from Srebrenica, then I knew the name, the last name --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll stop you there. Mr. Nikolic, that's precisely the point which I want to put to you. Let me put this to you as a question: Have you been consulting lots of documents in preparation for your testimony here, reading documents in preparation for your testimony?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I had no documents until I arrived here. No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who gave you the documents which you've been trying to refer to? You don't need to refer to them. Just tell us: Who gave you those documents?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I got the document -- well, his son would be here in the afternoon, he would be a witness, Kostadin Popovic, and then he'll explain that's where I got it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So Nikola Popovic gave you those documents?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you speak to Nikola Popovic about your testimony here in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He just handed you some documents without saying a word?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He didn't give it to me here, he gave it to me there, while we were still -- a month ago or two.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it right, Mr. Nikolic, that in Kravica, a lot of Serbs know that you are going to testify here; you've spoken a great deal to them about your testimony here, and they've suggested things that you should say here in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll break that down a bit. People in Kravica know that you're testifying here in The Hague against Naser Oric, don't they?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Because I -- they didn't know when they came to see me, these people from The Hague, two or three times, whether I'd go or not. Later I found out on Wednesday, and on Monday I was already here. Not much time had elapsed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So then how can Nikola Popovic gave you a document a month ago to bring to The Hague?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he gave it to me, he said, In case you go, you'll have it. He probably had it from his father. I'm not sure how it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you spoken to Jovan Nikolic about testifying here in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I won't pursue that.

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't seen Jovan Nikolic for at least six or seven months. I never go to Bratunac, and he doesn't even live there. I don't know where he's staying.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, going back to the prison briefly, you've told us that you lost weight while you were in Srebrenica. Did you see what the guards were eating in that they were getting a little better food than you?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't see.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you were released, isn't it right that a man with a left arm up to the elbow came to the prison and said that the first one to get up would be exchanged?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, two people came.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you recall whether one of those men was named Zele?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall that, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before you were released, you were with Ilija Ivanovic in hospital, weren't you, for a period.

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. Ilija was from a different village. He was in Bajina Basta, and I am in Zvornik. MR. DI FAZIO: I just don't think from the context that it's been understood by ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, I'll clarify that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I meant, in Srebrenica, weren't you and Ilija Ivanovic in hospital briefly before you were released, together in the hospital in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to move to a different area now altogether. You've told us, I believe - and correct me if I'm wrong - that you were not in the army, the Bosnian Serb army, after your release from captivity.

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I have an exhibit to pass up. It's from the Bratunac collection, and the ERN is 0131-9965. We see in English a list that refers to the infantry -- the 1st Infantry Battalion. If we look at the third page in the original.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to refer you to the third page, Mr. Nikolic, number 96, "Ratko Pajo Nikolic." Isn't that your name? Isn't that you? Number 96.

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My name, but the signature is not mine. I was not an able-bodied person; I couldn't have been in the army. I had a handicap earlier and after I'd been exchanged also. It was always like that. Back at the commands, they could have written whatever they liked. Maybe they had some other elderly people on their records too, when they collected money for whatever purpose. But I was incapable of serving in the military, even before I'd been exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'd ask that this document be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It will, of course, be given an exhibit number. However, I would like the witness to have his, or what appears to be a signature against his name on this document, on the third page, under 96, be shown to him. I think you need -- usher, you need to put it on the -- mark, as you did last time 96, with a piece of paper there, and then it will be moved towards the left. Yes. Mr. Nikolic, that last signature there, the very last one, the one on the bottom, do you recognise that signature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is it your signature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones. You want to give this document a number, and this will be D120.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, you've told us you weren't in the army because you were disabled, but you can hold a gun and you can guard a post, can't you? You told us you were in signals. Surely you could work in signals, even if you were disabled. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, his evidence was that he was a night watchman and he was retired for medical reasons in May of 1992. Nothing about his capacity to guard a post and nothing about his capacity to hold a weapon and --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's a question for him. MR. DI FAZIO: I know it is, but it's not his evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. You are right, Mr. Di Fazio. And incidentially, correct me if I'm wrong, but I get the impression, going through this document that you have just filed, that this refers to a period beginning from February --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, February 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So my question to you, Mr. Nikolic: Even in February 1995, you did not form part of the army, did you? In 1995, three years after these events, or two years after these events.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Finally, were you in the VRS in July 1995 when the genocide of Srebrenica's Bosnian Muslim population took place?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We have another document, a final document, to pass up. Bratunac collection, 0065-8822, and it's the second page -- that's the first page, and then 00658846, I think it is. Mr. Nikolic's name appears -- appears to appear twelfth from the bottom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, are you telling us you weren't in the VRS and weren't in the 1st Infantry Battalion of the Bratunac Brigade in July 1995? You can answer with a simple yes or no, after seeing that document.

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If that document -- there's no signature to compare, so if that could be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. That will carry the number D121. But one moment, because I -- if you look at the previous document, D120, under 96, which we showed to the witness, there is "Nikolic Pajo Ratko," which could coincide with the particulars that we have of the witness as confirmed in the first part of the examination-in-chief. If you look at this one, unless I am looking at someone else, which number were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, there aren't numbers, Your Honour, but it should be twelfth from the bottom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. It says "Nikolic, Mitra," --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm not sure we have the same --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There's another one, "Nikolic Pajo Ratko," okay. All right. But there is more than one Ratko Nikolic. Well, there's Rajko. There's Ratko yeah. All right. This is D121.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Finally, Mr. Nikolic, I put it to you that you didn't tell us -- I put it to you that you were in the 1st Infantry Battalion which was involved in mass killings in July 1995, but that you've denied this and you've exaggerated your mistreatment in Srebrenica to ease your conscience about the killings in which you were involved in 1995. That's my suggestion to you. In Kravica.

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Jones. Is there re-examination, Mr. Di Fazio? MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. Could the witness be shown D117, please. And I'd like the assistance of the usher to go to -- direct the attention of Mr. Nikolic to the page dealing with Opravdici, which has the ERN number ending 78. Re-examined by Mr. Di Fazio:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, Mr. Nikolic, I think you have part of a document that was shown to you by Defence counsel, and it deals with supposedly characters, or people, men, from Opravdici. You were talking about the age of some of those men. Can you just start -- there's only 16 of them. Just go down and tell the Trial Chamber the ages of those men, if you know them, and if you know their approximate age, also tell the Trial Chamber of their approximate age. So start at the top and let's go through it. Number 1, Mile Djukanovic?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mile Djukanovic, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't know him?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ranko, no. No, I don't know him at all. Stanko Gajic, no. Nikola. Nikola is working in Germany, he's not here. No. I don't know. Radislav --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know Nikola Gajic? Just yes or no, do you know Nikola Gajic?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Continue. Videsav Gajic; do you know that person?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Milivoje Cvetinovic; do you know that person?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Keep going down the list. Is there anyone there --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I suggest you keep going down the list, one by one. Otherwise we'll get confusion. MR. DI FAZIO: Sure. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Number 9, Zoran Nikolic, you're spoken about. Number 10, Slobodan Gavric --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I thought the object was to get the ages of these people. Presumably he knows --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do know Slobodan. MR. DI FAZIO: Well, okay. That's my next question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us how old in 1993? Do you know how old, approximately?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1993, no, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Just slow down and let's think about it. You've told us that you know Slobodan Gavric. Now --

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- back then, back then during the war, in 1993, about how old was he?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Slobodan, he was born around 1940. And he's bedridden now. For seven or eight years, he's been an invalid.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Go down to number 13, whose name, I think, is Miso -- I can't read that. It looks like Dukanovic. Do you know such a person?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do know him. Miso is an elderly man. He's about -- he's nearly 80 [as interpreted], and he walks with a stick. He walks worse than I do. I don't know Miladin. Miladin died.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I do apologise. There's a mistake in the transcript. I understood the witness to say an elderly man, meaning now, about 70, in the transcript it says 80. Could this be clarified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I think it needs to be clarified. This Dukanovic, Miso, the one who walks worse than you do, how old is he now, 70 or 80?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe he is 70. I haven't seen his documents. I don't know exactly. They were all older than me. I don't know when he was born.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's take the next one. Miladin Gavric, who is dead, how old was he at the time, in 1992/1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Miladin died. I can't explain anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but before he died he had an age. How old was he in 1992 or 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was elderly. No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Was he older than you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, older than me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. How much older than you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sure he was older. He had sons and grandchildren. About 70.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If he were still alive today -- you just passed 60; right? No, you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He would be how old if he were still alive today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If he was 70 then, he would be about 80 now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Yes. Next one. Bosko Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No what? Do you know this person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He's not a relative of yours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. He's no relation of mine. That's the village of Opravdici. It's 10 kilometres away. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Dragan Djukanovic. Did you know Dragan Djukanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I can't help you more than that, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you, Your Honour. That's just what I wanted to cover. Sorry, would Your Honours just bear with me for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of course. MR. DI FAZIO: Can the witness be shown D118, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: D118? MR. DI FAZIO: D118, I'm sorry. Yes, D118. And again, if the usher could assist, it's the second page, the page that Mr. Jones showed to the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Number 2240, 2240 is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Goran Nikolic. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Goran Nikolic. And that's the name of your son, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were asked about what your son was doing in October of 1992.

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My son is an electrical engineer, and he works in a company called Elektro Serbija in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thanks for telling us that. Now the question is: Was he doing that in October of 1992?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber if he was working at Elektro Serbija throughout 1992 or for just a part of 1992?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, throughout 1992, and he still works there. He's married there; he has a wife and two children. He lives there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he living in Belgrade in 1992, as well as working there?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: While we are still on this document, can anyone explain to me why, on the second page, after some names, you have the letter R and after some names you have the letter P?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, we think it probably refers to "poginuli" or "ranjeni." "Poginuli" being killed and "ranjeni" being wounded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think you were asked a question, but I will ask it again. Was your son Goran ever wounded during the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. I've finished with that document. Thank you, Ms. Usher.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were asked some questions about what you could see on the morning of the attack, and you said that initially you couldn't see any of the people over at Siljkovici because it was dawn or just breaking day. You've also testified in court that you did see armed men.

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, just -- okay. Now, just think back and tell the Trial Chamber about the time period, the time period that elapsed between your first waking up, going out to see the attack, what was happening, and the period of time when you first saw armed men. How much time elapsed between you being first made aware that something was happening and your first laying eyes on armed men? What sort of time period?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When my wife Marija got up at 5.30, I remember well, she entered the room and said, Ratko, Zoran, get up, there's an attack, we're surrounded. I went outside and you could hear shooting from all sides. We were being attacked from seven sides, Mandici, Opravdici, Popovici and the surrounding villages. Siljkovici, all of that was being attacked. And when it began to get light enough to see, at about 7.00, you could see the smoke and the flames rising from Siljkovici, and then Kravica started burning. And two hours later it had spread to all the Serbian villages.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. All I want to know is this, and you've gone some way to explaining it: About -- oh, I see. So are you saying it was about -- you knew that the attack had started, but it was about two and a half hours before you could see anything; is that what you're -- is that your evidence? Or could you see things clearly before 7.30?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at 5.30, as soon as I got up, we could hear the shooting and you could see the flames. There was red smoke rising up. It wasn't light yet, but you could see fires.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll leave this topic. You were also asked about the use of heavy weaponry by Mr. Jones, particularly around Kravica. Did any -- was any heavy weaponry - I mean mortars or artillery or cannons or big guns, not being rifles and automatic weapons - used right in the area of Zonjici, right where your house was and the houses of your neighbours? Any bombs land there?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You also mentioned that trucks were used to take away your wheat, TAM trucks. Did you see who was in those TAM trucks that was used to take away the wheat from your place, your -- Zonjici?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. All I saw was that my wheat was being driven away. When I got there in the evening, my wheat had been taken off. And there was a table there where they had had coffee. And you could see the tire tracks. And then the barn was set on fire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. But what the Trial Chamber needs to know is if you actually saw your wheat being loaded onto the trucks, or is it something that you've concluded because you saw the tire tracks and your wheat was gone? Do you understand what I mean? Is it something that you've figured out or something that you saw?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I saw it. They were arguing about my wheat. I was a bit further away. When they were gathering my wheat, I heard them arguing about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how many trucks, one or more?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't say. They had also horses with saddles and saddlebags. They were taking things, as much as they could carry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. Did you -- right. Are you saying that horses were used in Zonjici to take away goods?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were asked by Mr. Jones if guards had tried to stop people on occasions, or at least on one occasion, from beating you, and you answered yes. I want to know this: Are you saying --

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, when --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just wait for my question. Are you saying that guards continually tried to stop people beating you or did it on several occasions, or are you saying that guards only restrained people from attacking you once?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only once they prevented them. When he wanted to cut my throat here, the guard caught him by the hand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that's the one occasion when some restraint was -- came to your assistance.

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Nikolic. MR. DI FAZIO: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Di Fazio. Judge Brydensholt. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: When you, on the 7th of January, went back to Zvornik, to your own house, and then I understand you covered there, you stayed there until you were arrested, captured, on the 12th of January. During that time, you saw somebody taking away things, your wheat and other things, and you mentioned that it was civilians but also armed persons. Now, those armed persons who were there during those five days after the burning, where could they have stayed during nights? It was cold, I understand. There was no houses left in the village. Could they go home somewhere in the neighbourhood, or where did those people stay during nights, do you think?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These people I had occasion to see, because I was hiding by day, they held checkpoints, and in the evenings they called out to each other, in Zonjici, in Bacici, and in Opravdici. And there they had fires where they warmed themselves. I don't know whether they changed shifts, but they held those checkpoints and they had fires there. And I would hear them calling out to each other from Zonjici, to Bacici and so on. They were calling out to each other, communicating in that way. In Opravdici, there is still a bunker up there at the top, a dugout, in fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Judge Eser.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, I have a question with regard to captivity. Have you been told at any time for what reason you have been captured and detained?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Now, when you have been beaten, were you given any reason why you have been beaten?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Now, the beating, was it done completely silently, or did the people who beat you say something while they were beating you?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Judge Eser. I have got a few questions following up one of the questions that Judge Eser put to you which I had meant to put to you. Were you ever charged? You were detained, but were you ever charged? Were any accusations brought against you.

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Srebrenici, yes. There is a court there. They judged there. I have it here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think this is something -- this is something that we need. So, in other words, let's see this document. Usher, could you bring it over, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, we just wish to express our concern that the witness seems to be relying on documents for his testimony --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, we'll see what this is.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: -- and we haven't seen them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is a document that we saw yesterday. This is a document that we have two versions of. One is yours and one is the Prosecution's.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Exactly. We'd be interested in which version the witness has.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is the -- now --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: In other words, is it the one with Razmjena and without the date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Without the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm obliged, Your Honour. MR. DI FAZIO: I might invite Your Honours to ask this witness when he got that particular document that he's showing you in court and who gave it to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Who gave you this document, Mr. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nikola Popovic gave it to me two months ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It appears to have the ERN number. How did Nikola Popovic get a document with the ERN number, Mr. Di Fazio? MR. DI FAZIO: Can I ask some questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think if you help to clear this mess up, it will better.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, it may be a matter for Nikola Popovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. But maybe Mr. Di Fazio is going to tell us that he handed it to Mr. Popavic and Mr. Popovic handed it to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Anything is possible, Your Honour. MR. DI FAZIO: Anything is possible, Your Honour, and Mr. Popovic of course can be asked about this, and rightly should be. Further Re-examination by Mr. Di Fazio:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, when you came to The Hague here, were you shown a number of documents and asked questions about them by myself?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did I show you a number of documents that concerned you personally?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you interested in those documents?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ask for copies of those documents?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, is the document that you handed to Their Honours such a document, one that was shown to you here in The Hague, or did Nikola Popovic --

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, you know that you've told Their Honours --

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was shown to me and Nikola gave it to me, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So that's your position. Fine. MR. DI FAZIO: I can't go any further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think we need to go any further, because he considers this as a charge. You can give it back. Questioned by the Court: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The other question that I wanted to ask you: Did you ever receive any kind of compensation for the damage your property sustained?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Or for the losses that you sustained, the produce --

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- cattle, nothing. So since the war, since these events, you have not been compensated in any way?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. I received nothing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Now, this Zulfo Tursunovic, after your exchange, did you ever see Zulfo again in your life, after you were exchanged?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Did you ever see any photo of him?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the other person, Naser Oric, that you mentioned and that you described in your statement, that you mentioned here during your testimony, did you ever see him again, after you were exchanged?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Did you ever see any pictures of him, any photo of him? Did you ever see him on TV, for example?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have seen photographs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Have you been shown photographs by the Prosecution of this person?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You haven't got these photos with you, have you?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Where did you see these photos?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the newspapers. When he went to The Hague, then I saw the newspaper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And you recognised him as the Naser Oric that you had seen in the van?

utterances.speaker: RATKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I have no further questions, which basically means that your testimony ends here. Mr. Nikolic, on behalf of Judge Brydensholt and Judge Eser and on my own behalf and on behalf of the Tribunal, I should like to thank you for having come over to give testimony in this case. You will be attended to by our usher. I apologise once more to you for having kept you here for an entire week, but it was necessary. The usher will -- and the other officers of the Tribunal will attend to you, and you will receive all the assistance you require to enable you to return home, to return home. The last thing we need to tell you is to wish you a safe journey.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, one matter, if the witness could be firmly instructed not to speak to Nikola Popovic in the meantime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you for -- I had it in my mind before, and I forgot all about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thanks, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I must also warn you, Mr. Nikolic, that although you have finished your testimony, I don't want you to contact Mr. Popovic or any member of his family. Do you understand me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I also don't want you to contact anyone who would, in turn, contact Mr. Popovic. You must not send any messages to Mr. Popovic directly or indirectly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you. You may leave. Usher, you can escort the witness --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, thank you. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we can have the break now. And again, we require 30 minutes to go on with the work that we started before. Thank you. So we'll meet at five minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. This next witness does not enjoy any protective measures, does he?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour. Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: No, this witness does not require protective measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thought so.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Also because he was being mentioned by the previous witness in any case.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, in addition, for the record, my name is Jan Wubben, lead counsel for the Prosecution, together with Ms. Joanne Richardson, taking over from our colleagues this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, Mr. Popovic, and welcome to this Tribunal. I take it that you are receiving interpretation of what I am saying in your own language? In other words, you are understanding what is being said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. You are about to start giving evidence, and before you do so, our Rules require that you enter a solemn declaration, equivalent to an oath, to the effect that in the course of your testimony, you will be speaking the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text of this solemn declaration is contained on a piece of paper that Madam Usher will be handing to you. Please read it out aloud, and that will be your solemn undertaking with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Popovic. You may sit down. As I told you already, we will be starting with your testimony today. We will probably not finish it, which will mean that you will need to come back tomorrow. And the procedure that we will follow is that you will first be asked a series of questions by Ms. Richardson. Is that correct, Ms. Richardson?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, indeed, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And when that is over, she will be followed by Madam Vidovic, who is appearing as Defence lead counsel for Naser Oric. In terms of your solemn declaration, you have a duty, an obligation, to treat the Prosecution and the Defence along the same lines, the same. You have no right to distinguish or to discriminate against any one of them. They are here to do their duty, and your obligation is to answer all the questions that are put to you, whoever puts the questions to you, truthfully and fully. Have I made myself understood? Okay. Having said that, I hand him to you, Ms. Richardson, and you can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Just one matter before we get started, I notice that the witness was informed that we are continuing tomorrow. Is that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Not tomorrow, because tomorrow is Plenary. We will continue the day after tomorrow, the day after tomorrow, because tomorrow we have -- all the Judges of this Tribunal have a very long day in which they will discuss many important matters. So there will be no time for any sittings tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Examined by Ms. Richardson:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Popovic, good afternoon. Please state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC
utterances.text: Nikola Popovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And please confirm the following information: That you were born in December 1974; you are married with two children; you are of Serb ethnicity; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in 1992, and until 1993, of January, you were a baker, and that you are presently working as a construction worker; and that you also do some farming as well.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You live in the village of Kravica; in fact, you were born there. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you lived there in 1992 as well, and January of 1993.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And during that time period, you resided in Kravica with your parents, grandfather, and sisters.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if you could tell us a little bit about Kravica. Could you tell us if it is a Serb village, and whether or not the surrounding -- and how many houses make up the village of Kravica?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Kravica is a purely Serb village. In the villages around Kravica, there were between 40 and 50. As for the inhabitants, in my estimate, which is a rough estimate, I think around 1.000 inhabitants. Houses, I would say a total of between 700 and 800 houses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, were there any Muslims -- let me rephrase that question. Where is the closest Muslim village?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC
utterances.text: It was Sandici. Sandici, the Muslim village, two and a half or three kilometres from Kravica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us what most people in Kravica do for a living, at least what they did in 1992 up until January of 1993? Were they farmers, or did they have other types of jobs?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC
utterances.text: In Kravica, most people were farmers and bred livestock, for the most part.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, if I could have the usher's assistance, with Your Honours' permission, I'd like to have the witness look at a map. And if we could have an exhibit number as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This will be P45 ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, it will be P455.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Popovic, if you could just look at that map that's on the ELMO, and could you circle where Kravica is located on that map.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you point to the surrounding Serb villages that are in the immediate vicinity of Kravica.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC
utterances.text: Serb or Muslim? Muslim?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, first -- well, why don't we do this: Why don't you point to the Muslim village that you just testified about, that was the closest to Kravica.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Indicates].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And then if you can, please point to the surrounding villages, or the surrounding Serb villages, in the immediate vicinity of Kravica.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Indicates].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. If I could ask the usher to give the witness another coloured pen, and if you could just circle those quickly for us. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you could hand crayons in different colours --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I think we have a red pen now with the witness, so ...

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I think that that is sufficient for now, unless there's another one that you can see immediately.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. For the record, the witness has circled in red several villages and hamlets that appear on the map -- on the map, in the vicinity of Kravica. Witness, could I ask you to sign this map at the top right-hand corner, please, in the white space that there is.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, one matter is that the witness was still circling villages, and the only reason I mention is that because, for example, in the meantime he's circled Brezanci, and that's a name we've seen. So I wouldn't want the witness to feel that he had to stop if he still had --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Jones. So sign the map at the top right-hand corner, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What am I supposed to do next?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just sign your name, put your signature.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Popovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Now, go back to the map. You were -- when I interrupted you, you were still in the process of putting a circle in red around certain villages. Are there any other villages or hamlets that you would like to mark on that map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, please. I need to have a closer look.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't see the village of Marici on this map. I can't find it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it in -- well, maybe what you could do is just put an X where you approximate it would be if it was on the map, in the vicinity of those villages.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, the village of Glogova, is that also a Serb village?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it mixed or is it Muslim?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC
utterances.text: It's a Muslim village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned Sandici previously. If you could - and I will hand a blue pen to the usher - if you could just circle the Muslim village of Sandici. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the two other villages in that vicinity, Urkovici, I may not be pronouncing it correctly, but is that a Serb or a Muslim village?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC
utterances.text: Brncici [phoen]. A Muslim village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Could you circle that, please. It's very close to Sandici. Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]. Yes. Krncici too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that's also Muslim?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC
utterances.text: And there's another village here in between Pajici. It's a big village, a Muslim village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I think that's sufficient for now with respect to the immediate area of Kravica. Could you tell us, is it correct that Kravica is located in a valley?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, with respect to 1992, I would like to ask about your service with the Serb army, if in fact, you did serve with them. Did there come a time in 1992 that you were mobilised by the Serb army?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was mobilised as a logistics person. I was a baker. I had never done my regular military service, but that counted as military service eventually.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you paid by the Serb military? Did you receive any money?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were two or three salaries. About June, three salaries. It wasn't a lot of money, really.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember what month you were mobilised by the Serb military, that you received notice that you were mobilised?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC
utterances.text: It may have been May, May 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How old were you at that time?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you receive any uniforms or weapons as a part of this mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC
utterances.text: No, I received no uniform or weapons. Those of us who worked at the bakery had a rifle; that was always there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did working at the bakery entail? Could you just tell us briefly. Were you a baker, and did you have to deliver bread to other people in Kravica, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was a bakery in my own house, attached to my own house. When the war began, a bakery was built of brick, and this catered for the entire village. We baked bread there, and all the villagers came to our bakery for bread. It was next to the school building. So that was for the entire village of Kravica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you already a baker by the time -- when you received the mobilisation notice?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I completed my eight years of elementary school, and I found a job at Kravica. A relative of mine, Popovic, opened this big bakery. I worked there for a year and a half or two years, and then the war began and caught me there at the bakery, in Kravica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were other men in Kravica, to your knowledge, also mobilised? Did other men receive mobilisation notice from the Serb army?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. People were mobilised, after the war had begun in the areas of Bratunac and Srebrenica. I think it was May, late April or early May, when the first man was wounded in Jerkovici, before the war had begun for real. The man was Andrija Jerkovic, and he was wounded in late April.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were men mobilised? Excuse me. Were men in Kravica also mobilised?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With respect to the men that were mobilised, other than yourself, do you know if they also were paid or received their salary from the Serb army?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know where the salaries came from, but it kept on coming for two or three months. Someone obviously secured some money. It wasn't much money, but we received an amount in the whereabouts of 10 to 20 German marks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did the other men that were also mobilised, did they receive any weapons or uniforms in addition to anything else? Whether the salaries came from them or not, do you know if there were weapons or uniforms issued by the Serb army?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC
utterances.text: To start with, there was some sort of training. Some weapons arrived, and there was training on a large meadow. And some were issued with weapons and other weapons were returned. But there weren't enough weapons for the entire village, not for all the inhabitants.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember when the training took place, and where the training took place?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC
utterances.text: It was on a large meadow, for four or five days. After that, it finished, and they collected and moved on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know when this training took place? Was it in 1992?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly when, but it was in 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, was it in the summer or the spring?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC
utterances.text: It was summer. It was late spring or early summer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you also trained?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC
utterances.text: No. I didn't go -- undergo any training, but I did go up to the big meadow. However, I wasn't trained.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did all of the men who participated in the training receive weapons at some point; do you know?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC
utterances.text: Not all of them, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did there come a time that your village, Kravica, established a village guard?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was a village guard there. The guard was kept in Kravica until the war began to spread. When the war began to spread, and the Muslims from Kravica, Konjevic Polje, attacked, then a village defence was put up. Then people were deployed in villages. This started to spread. The villages started to burn.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Before we get to the villages burning, let's talk a little bit more about the village guard. Do you remember when in 1992, what month, this village guard was established in Kravica? And are we talking about the town of Kravica or the surrounding villages that make up Kravica?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC
utterances.text: I know about Kravica. I don't know about the other villages. I only know about Kravica, where I lived. When things started heating up, there were village guards, people who stayed awake at nights in the village. They were awake and they watched.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who were these people?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC
utterances.text: People from the village of Kravica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how many of them were there?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC
utterances.text: It would change. There were always four or five people awake in the village, standing at the centre, because things were brewing and somebody had to be awake in the village, check the traffic, and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did they guard in the village?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC
utterances.text: The village, the entire village; the school, the health centre, the post office, the health centre, the local office. All the facilities in the center of Kravica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you also part of this village guard?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC
utterances.text: No. I was young. And at that time Muslim inhabitants would take down the Serbian flag, they would write graffiti, "SDA", and things were really brewing, they were heating up, so somebody had to be there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, was your father or grandfather a member of the village guard?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which one?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC
utterances.text: My father was in the village guard, not my grandfather, because he was 72, he was not liable for military service.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the village guard have uniforms, and did they have weapons?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC
utterances.text: No, there were no weapons, except if people were hunters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you just mentioned that things heated up. Could you just explain to us, what are you referring to in terms of things heating up? Are you referring to what occurred in other villages or in the village of Kravica?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC
utterances.text: As I've just said, a man was wounded, Andrija Jerkovic. In his village of Jerkovici, he was mowing a meadow, and the Muslims attacked him there and wounded him. And then up there in Magasici, Stojko Popovic was killed. That was in April, April or early May. End of April, early May. That's when it started to ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Popovic, did there come a time that when the village established a defence line, or the village of Kravica and the surrounding villages establish a defence line?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. There was a defence line, and people were in the villages. It was the people who were from a certain village that held the defence there; Kravica, Siljkovici. When people started getting killed, then people took this seriously, and this spread.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know when this was established, this defence line?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know the precise date, but I think it was in early May.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: If I could just have the usher's assistance with the map that was just placed on the ELMO, Prosecution Exhibit 455.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Popovic, please take a look at the map and tell us -- and if you could draw exactly where the defence line was set up that included the village of Kravica, maybe with a blue pen. I think that would be appropriate. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC
utterances.text: At the beginning of the war? Should I draw a line as to the villages we guarded and secured?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]. I do apologise. A little while ago I circled a Muslim village here. Hadzici, that's a Muslim village. I only realised that now. I thought it was another village, but I now see it's Hadzici, a Muslim village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you take an X and just X out -- well, not cross out but just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go over the red circle in blue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just circle it now in blue, if you will, with the same pen. You can just circle that same village in blue. The village that you just put an X through, can you circle it in blue, Mr. Popovic.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. So the line that you just drew on Prosecution Exhibit 455, this represented the defence line. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, could you tell us why this line was established?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC
utterances.text: Because the war had already started, and we'd already had two or three victims in our village of Kravica. It had already started. And that's why the village defence line was put up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the purpose was to defend the village, the villages, within that line?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, to defend the village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how many men were in the defence line, or participated in this defence line?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know the exact number, how many there were when the war broke out. I can't tell you exactly. I don't know exactly how many men were there in 1992, when it all started. Later, people left. A lot of people from Kravica were killed or wounded, so they were scattered after the beginning of the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there men from Kravica also in this defence line?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC
utterances.text: They were all men from Kravica, the local villagers from Kravica. There was nobody from the outside at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So there were no -- there was -- I'll withdraw -- rephrase the question. This defence line and the men that were part of it, did this also include Serbs outside of Kravica, serving in the Serb army?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC
utterances.text: These were all Serbs from Kravica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Not from -- not outside of Kravica, in other words.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand your question. Could you repeat it, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's fine. My question is: Other than the men from Kravica on this defence line, did the Serb military send additional men to assist with this defence line?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC
utterances.text: It did when the attack had already started. When the villages were already attacked and when they'd started burning, that was when help arrived.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you referring to January of 1993 or December of 1992? Could you be more specific? When did they send this help?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC
utterances.text: No, I'm talking about 1992. Because there are villages here that were burnt before December and before Christmas. On the 7th of January, half of the villages were burnt before. We had fierce attacks on the 20th of July in Magasici, and they attacked Jezestica on the 20th of July, and seven civilians were killed in Magasici. Seven civilians, five women, and a girl who was pregnant, she was eight months' pregnant, and she was -- she was a relative of my wife, so I know that. And in Jezestica, people were killed. And then this spread to the other villages, Banovici, Ocenovici, Lipenovici, Jasikovaca, Dolovi, Mratinjci, Donji Mratinjci, Gornji Jerkovici, Brana, Donji Brana. These were all the villages that were burnt between May and December.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Is it convenient for you to stop here, Ms. Richardson?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So we will adjourn until the day after tomorrow. Tomorrow is Plenary day so we won't be able to sit. And we will be sitting on Thursday, in the afternoon, in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I understand that's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. You will have time to rest. You will be attended to during your stay here. What I want to make sure is that you do not contact anyone between now and Thursday when you continue your evidence, you do not contact anyone in relation to the events that you are testifying about.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And you must not let others contact you either.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So our sitting is adjourned. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
